presentingComplaint: Acute severe cramping lower-abdominal pain and marked bloating for 12 hours, brought to the emergency department by a worried partner.
history: 32-year-old marketing executive presents with a 12-hour episode of severe, crampy, colicky lower-abdominal pain with visible bloating and an urge to open her bowels, on the background of a demanding, sleep-deprived work week. During the episode she also developed palpitations, a pounding chest and a sense of impending doom while sitting in the waiting room, prompting the triage team to consider an acute intra-abdominal catastrophe and a cardiac/panic event in parallel. On careful history she has had this abdominal pain intermittently for over 4 years: recurrent lower-abdominal cramping present on average 2-3 days per week, characteristically RELIEVED by passing stool or flatus and associated with a change in stool form and frequency. She alternates between periods of loose, more frequent stools and periods of harder, pellet-like stools with straining (IBS-mixed pattern), with a subjective sense of incomplete evacuation and mucus in the stool. Symptoms flare with stress, caffeine and skipped meals and settle when she is on holiday. She denies any weight loss, nocturnal diarrhoea waking her from sleep, rectal bleeding or black stools, fevers or family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. No recent travel, no antibiotics, no sick contacts. Last menstrual period 2 weeks ago, cycle regular. She has previously been extensively investigated (normocytic normal FBC, negative coeliac serology, normal colonoscopy age 30 done for reassurance) and carries a working diagnosis of IBS. Todays acute severity and the concurrent palpitations are what is new and frightening to her.
examination: Alert, anxious, hyperventilating intermittently. Abdomen is soft with generalised mild lower-abdominal tenderness and audible normal bowel sounds; palpable, non-tender faecal loading in the left iliac fossa; NO guarding, rigidity, rebound or peritonism, no palpable mass, no organomegaly. Hernial orifices intact, PR examination normal with no blood and soft brown stool. No pallor, no lymphadenopathy, no peripheral oedema. Pain is reproducible on palpation and eases after she passes flatus during the assessment. Cardiorespiratory examination unremarkable aside from sinus tachycardia; peripheries warm and well perfused.
imaging: Erect chest and supine abdominal X-ray: no free air, no dilated bowel loops or air-fluid levels, moderate faecal loading in the descending/sigmoid colon. Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis (performed given the acute severity): no obstruction, no bowel-wall thickening, patent mesenteric vessels with no arterial/venous occlusion, normal appendix, no free fluid or collection, normal ovaries.
microbiology: Not indicated; no fever, no diarrhoeal illness, no travel. Stool studies not sent as there is no acute infective diarrhoea.
differentialDiagnoses: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-mixed), acute symptom flare (final diagnosis)
Acute mesenteric ischaemia (excluded by normal lactate and CT angiographic phase)
Panic attack contributing to concurrent palpitations
finalDiagnosis: Irritable bowel syndrome (Rome IV, mixed subtype) presenting as an acute symptom flare with a concurrent anxiety/panic episode; no organic emergency identified.
citations: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) — Clinical Guideline: Management of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (2021)
British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) — Guidelines on the management of irritable bowel syndrome (2021)
Rome Foundation — Rome IV Diagnostic Criteria for Functional Bowel Disorders (2016)
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Irritable Bowel Syndrome
stewardship: Non-infective functional disorder: NO antibiotics or antimicrobials indicated. Management is positive diagnosis on Rome IV criteria after excluding alarm features, patient education and reassurance, dietary modification (regular meals, reduced caffeine, trial of a dietitian-led low-FODMAP diet), soluble fibre and antispasmodics for pain, laxatives/anti-diarrhoeals titrated to the predominant bowel pattern, and addressing the psychological/anxiety component (relaxation, CBT, or gut-brain neuromodulators such as low-dose tricyclics if refractory). Avoid opioids (worsen motility, gut dysfunction) and avoid repeated imaging/endoscopy once a confident diagnosis is made.
contraindications: Avoid empirical antibiotics — no infective process; unnecessary exposure risks C. difficile and resistance
Avoid opioid analgesia — worsens constipation, bloating and narcotic bowel syndrome
Avoid repeated CT imaging for recurrent functional flares — cumulative radiation with no diagnostic yield
Do not label as IBS without first excluding alarm features (weight loss, GI bleeding, anaemia, age >50 new onset, family history of colorectal cancer/IBD)
edgeCases: Acute severity plus concurrent palpitations can mimic an intra-abdominal or cardiac emergency — normal lactate, normal CT and a normal troponin reassure while chronic Rome IV features confirm IBS
Raised faecal calprotectin would mandate reconsideration of IBD; here it is normal (<50 ug/g)
New-onset symptoms after age 50 or any alarm feature would require colonoscopy before attributing to IBS
IBS and anxiety/panic disorder frequently coexist (gut-brain axis); treating one without the other leads to relapse
expectedMaiK: Recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation with a change in stool form/frequency over years, no alarm features, and a normal acute organic workup (lactate, CT, calprotectin, troponin) point to an IBS flare with a superimposed panic episode rather than a surgical or vascular emergency.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the abdominal pain relieved by defecation, and is it associated with a change in stool frequency or form (Rome IV)?
Are there any alarm features — unintentional weight loss, rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, or family history of colorectal cancer/IBD?
How long have symptoms been present and do they fluctuate with stress, diet or the menstrual cycle?
What is the predominant stool pattern (constipation, diarrhoea, or mixed) to guide subtype-specific therapy?
Are the palpitations/chest symptoms part of recurrent anxiety or panic episodes?
expectedInvestigations: Serum lactate and contrast CT abdomen to exclude mesenteric ischaemia/obstruction in this acute presentation
TSH and beta-hCG as clinically indicated
regressionAssertions: stewardship.tier must be null and antibiotics must be empty (non-infective functional disorder)
Must recommend faecal calprotectin and screening for alarm features before diagnosing IBS
Normal lactate and CT must be used to exclude mesenteric ischaemia and bowel obstruction
Must NOT recommend antibiotics or opioid analgesia
